analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to disclose the wage range when hiring and to current employees, with penalties for violations.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat without any action in the House Education and Workforce Committee since its referral in March 2025, with two Democratic cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to make it an unfair labor practice for an employer to post a job without stating the wage or wage range, to refuse to tell an applicant the range before discussing pay, or to decline to tell a current employee their range at hire and at least yearly. It would also make retaliation against workers for using these rights unlawful, with civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation and statutory damages of $1,000 to $10,000 per affected worker, enforceable in court including on behalf of groups of similarly situated workers. The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and has had no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Job applicants and current employees would gain the right to see the pay range for any job before applying, interviewing, or negotiating, and the right to their own range on request at hire and annually. Workers in low-wage and female- or minority-dominated roles, who are most likely to be underpaid relative to unknowable internal scales, would benefit most from the information and from the damages and attorneys' fees the bill creates for violations.

how_it_helps.text: Employers must post the wage or wage range in any public or internal job posting, and must tell any applicant the range before discussing compensation and whenever asked.
Current employees must be told the wage range for their position at hire and at least once a year, and whenever they ask.

Retaliation against workers who use these rights is unlawful, and workers can recover statutory damages of $1,000 to $10,000 per violation plus attorneys' fees, in actions brought on behalf of similarly situated coworkers.

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the cost: they must research and publish good-faith wage ranges, maintain them across postings and reviews, and face civil penalties and private lawsuits — including class-style actions by similarly situated workers — when they fail.

drawbacks.text: Employers would face new compliance and litigation exposure: up to $10,000 in civil penalties per violation plus statutory damages of $1,000–$10,000 per affected worker, which could be pursued in class-style actions on behalf of similarly situated applicants.

The good-faith 'anticipated' wage range standard is flexible, so employers could post wide or loosely grounded ranges that satisfy the letter of the law without revealing what a candidate might actually be offered.

The bill has attracted only two cosponsors in a chamber where the majority party has not supported federal pay-disclosure mandates, and states and cities with such laws are largely large blue jurisdictions, so opponents could argue a national mandate imposes costs where local rules do not.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to workers—knowable pay ranges, better negotiating position, less room for discriminatory pay gaps—are real and the compliance burden on employers is modest, since most large employers already operate salary bands internally. The main honest drawback is the penalty structure: statutory damages and class actions could generate litigation even where no worker was actually underpaid, and small employers might respond by posting vague ranges or shifting hiring outside the covered process. On balance it is a low-cost rule that shifts information power from employers to workers, but as introduced it never moved, so its costs and benefits remain untested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee in March 2025 and no action has been taken on it since.

narrative.text: The Salary Transparency Act was introduced in the House on March 10, 2025 and referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.
Since that referral, the bill's action history shows no hearings, no markups, no votes, and no further movement.
The bill attracted only two cosponsors, both House Democrats, and no Republican support is recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has lost or gained a new right, since nothing has been voted on; employers continue operating under existing, mostly state-level pay-disclosure rules.

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.what_they_did: Controls the committee where the bill sits and has not advanced it; no Republican cosponsors are recorded.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has only Democratic cosponsors (2), and as a delegate-sponsored bill with no committee action it has never drawn a party-line test vote.

industries.industry: Employers (businesses and public agencies subject to the Fair Labor Standards Act)
industries.note: They would have to publish pay ranges for openings, report ranges to current employees yearly, and face civil penalties and worker lawsuits for violations. Their interest in keeping pay opaque runs against workers' ability to comparison-shop and negotiate.
They gain a legal right to see the pay range for any job before committing to it, with damages and attorneys' fees to enforce it.

analysis.trajectory: With a referral to committee in March 2025, two cosponsors, and no movement since, the usual path for a bill like this is to sit until the Congress ends. Advancement would require the Education and Workforce Committee majority to schedule a hearing or markup, which the party composition does not suggest is likely.
